title: Coalesced weight stripping and kernel fastpath specification
content:
Purpose:
This doc specifies a pragmatic runtime for minimizing cold-token latency and transient memory overhead when loading large model shards. It focuses on two coordinated mechanisms that together reduce end-to-end latency for first tokens and make hot-swap safer: 1) coalesced weight stripping (compact in-memory staging of only the essential kernel-friendly slices) and 2) kernel fastpath warmup (coordinated, minimal kernel priming sequence triggered by staged prefetch events). The policy is KV-cache aware: eviction and prefetch decisions are made jointly with KV residency needs so that we do not thrash on both weights and cache simultaneously.

Background and motivation:
- Cold starts for large sharded models remain a dominant source of tail latency for low-QPS endpoints and bursty workloads.
- Full mmap’ing or eager eager-loading entire shards is expensive in IO and memory working set.
- Existing lazy chunk-loading reduces memory footprint but often leaves kernels unprimed and causes expensive first inference paths.
- KV cache pressure and weight residency compete; naive eviction layers cause regressions when both weights and KV are evicted on a single node during spikes.

Design goals (measurable):
- Reduce 95th-percentile token latency on cold sessions by >= 30% versus current lazy chunk loader under a 1-rps ephemeral workload.
- Bound transient memory overhead during staging to < 5% of GPU RAM for models up to 70B under typical shard layouts.
- Ensure hot-swap of a model variant completes atomically from the caller’s perspective and provides integrity guarantees (checksum + staged commit).
- Coordinate KV cache residency so that prefetching weights does not evict hot KV entries critical for ongoing sessions.

Core ideas (high level):
1) Coalesced weight stripping (CWS): on-disk shards are logically sliced into micro-fragments (alignment ~ 4–16KB depending on tensor alignment). When a request references a range of layers/kernels, the loader computes a minimal set of fragments that contain kernel hot-path parameters (attention q/k/v/out projections, rotary/sinusoidal tables, feedforward first linear) and assembles these into a compact, transient in-GPU buffer (staging ring). The staging buffer uses packed, page-aligned descriptors so kernels can access contiguous memory for the most latency-sensitive ops without requiring full tensor materialization.

2) Kernel fastpath warmup: once CWS has staged the minimal kernel slices, a controlled warmup sequence runs a tiny synthetic micro-batch through the new kernels to fill kernel-specific internal buffers and to populate per-kernel heuristics (e.g., attention key precomputation state). Warmup is runtime-limited (e.g., 50–200ms budget) and prioritized by request latency SLOs. Warmup uses a lightweight input signature generator that replays minimal context tokens derived from the caller’s prompt fingerprint to avoid producing sensitive content.

3) KV-cooperative eviction and soft-probation: eviction policy is extended to include an eviction score that weights both weight-residency benefit and live KV cache pressure. When memory is needed, candidates enter a soft-probation stage where their fragments can be evicted from staging but kept in a compressed cold-resident mmap mapping (zero-copy fallback). If eviction would remove fragments that a hot KV entry references (based on recent traces), eviction is deprioritized for a short probation window (configurable, default 10s).

4) Hot-swap commit with integrity proofs: hot-swap of a model variant proceeds through a three-phase handshake: prepare -> staged-validate -> atomic-commit. Prepare prefetches CWS fragments for the new variant into an isolated staging namespace. Staged-validate runs checksum/shape validation and one or two fastpath warmups. Atomic-commit switches routing pointers and marks old psyche entries for background reclamation. If a validation failure occurs, rollback is automatic to the previous routing pointer. All stages are logged to the serving runtime’s transaction log for observability and rollback audit.

Mechanics and protocol details:
- Fragment layout: fragments are identified by <shard-id, fragment-offset, fragment-length>. Fragment boundaries are aligned to 4KB on disk; in-memory staging buffers align to GPU page size to enable best DMA paths. Fragments are represented by an immutable descriptor that includes a 64-bit checksum.

- Staging ring: a per-GPU circular allocator exposed to kernels via a fast descriptor table. Staging buffers are short lived (target TTL 60–600s). The allocator supports eviction callbacks so the runtime can notify kernel owners of descriptor invalidation (neutralizing stale pointers).

- Prefetch triggers: three distinct triggers start coalesced prefetch: a) synchronous request referencing layers not resident in full, b) low-latency canary proactively started by the router for routes with rising QPS, c) scheduled warmup for canary variants in canary rollouts. Requests that arrive while staging is in progress are given priority for fastpath warmup and are routed to partial-execution paths that can leverage staged descriptors.

- Kernel integration: kernels that opt in to the fastpath expose a minimal runtime binding to the staging descriptor table (thin API: lookup(descriptor_id) -> device_ptr + stride + shape). Kernels must implement a quick null-check and register a destructor callback so that if the descriptor is invalidated owners can flush any derived state. Kernels that do not implement the binding will fallback to the legacy path (full tensor materialization).

- mmap + safetensors behavior: disk-backed safetensors remain the canonical source of truth. The loader maintains an mmapped view for each shard file but only materializes fragment mappings with mmap_madvise(MADV_WILLNEED) when prefetch is requested. A zero-copy fallback path uses the mmap page directly if CWS fails to stage due to memory pressure; in that case the kernel must accept higher latency but correct execution. All frag descriptors encode an expected safetensors byte-range and digest; staged-validate performs a quick digest compare against the mmapped range before promoting staged fragments to the fastpath.

- Eviction and admission control: admission to the staging ring requires an admission score computed from: (expected QPS benefit, recent hits on the fragment, KV-affinity score, memory cost). Fragments with low admission and high eviction score may be refused and instead rely on mmap fallback. Admission policy parameters are exposed to the optimizer subsystem for autotuning based on historical traces.

Telemetry and metrics (minimum set):
- staged_fragments.count (per model, per node)
- staged_fragments.memory_bytes (gauge)
- kernel_fastpath.warmup_latency_ms.p50/p95/p99
- admission.rejects.per_minute
- eviction.probation_hits
- hot_swap.prepare_time_ms, hot_swap.commit_time_ms, hot_swap.rollback_count
- kv_cooperative.eviction_conflicts_resolved

Operational playbook (short):
- Canary rollout: enable CWS fastpath on a small pool of low-traffic routes with synthetic traffic monitors. Compare 95p latency and cold start counts over a 48–72 hour window.
- On observed increased evictions that correlate with KV-miss spikes, temporarily raise probation window or lower admission thresholds for reloading weight fragments.
- If checksum mismatches detected in staged-validate, fail the prepare and investigate upstream artifact publication processes.

Safety, data handling and privacy notes:
- Warmup inputs must be fingerprint derived and never contain customer-provided PII. The warmup generator must be reviewed by security to ensure no leakage.
- Staging buffers are ephemeral and cleared on any node restart or variant commit. Checksums and transaction logs are kept for audit but do not include raw weights.

Implementation roadmap (phased):
- Phase 0 (prototype, 2 sprint): minimal CWS library that reads safetensors ranges, builds a staging buffer, and exposes the descriptor table. Simple kernel shim for attention qkv.
- Phase 1 (integration, 4 sprint): kernel fastpath warmups for attention + MLP, KV-cooperative eviction signals integrated with existing KV controller, telemetry dashboard.
- Phase 2 (hardening, 3 sprint): safe hot-swap handshake, admission autotuning, canary rollout tooling and rollback automation.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- Staging TTL tuning is workload dependent; what heuristics best correlate TTL with long-tail request lifetimes?
- How much synthetic warmup (number of tokens) yields best tradeoff between warmup cost and latency improvement for transformer variants with very different layer widths?
- Interplay between staged fragment compression and kernel memory layout: compressed staging reduces memory but increases warmup CPU/GPU compute. When to decompress?

Appendix: quick example flow (request path):
1) Router receives request referencing model:v3.2 (not fully resident).
2) Loader computes fragment set via static index -> issues coalesced prefetch into staging ring.
3) Staging allocates descriptors and returns descriptor ids.
4) Kernel fastpath binding resolves descriptor ids and initiates warmup micro-batch using an anonymized fingerprint.
5) Post-warmup, the request proceeds on fastpath and receives normal inference latency.
6) If subsequent memory pressure arises, fragments enter probation and may be evicted to mmap fallback; eviction events are surfaced to telemetry.

Contact and reviewers:
- Owning engineer: Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood.ai)
- Reviewers: Liam Chen, Marcos Rivera, Sofia Nguyen

Notes: This spec intentionally favors a pragmatic, incremental surface area to reduce blast radius. It targets the subset of kernels that dominate first-token latency and defers full tensor materialization to fallback paths. Feedback welcome—looking for implementation owners for Phase 0 and Phase 1.
